person.name: Antoni_Gaudí
person.summary: Antoni Gaudí i Cornet was a Catalan architect and designer, the leading figure of Catalan Modernisme. Working largely in Barcelona, he developed a highly personal style rooted in natural forms, craft traditions, and an increasingly intense Catholic spirituality. He is best known for transforming the Sagrada Família into his lifelong project.

chapters.headline: Forged in Catalonia
chapters.bridge_statement: A restless talent leaves the workshop world behind, searching for a city big enough to hold his ambitions.

chapters.headline: A Genius Enters Barcelona
chapters.bridge_statement: Credentials open doors, but it’s patronage, risk, and obsession that begin to shape the legend.
involved_people: Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano

chapters.headline: Stone Becomes Living Form
chapters.bridge_statement: As the city applauds, his architecture grows stranger, freer, and more alive with movement.

chapters.headline: Single-Will Cathedral
chapters.bridge_statement: With everything else stripped away, one project absorbs his days, his body, and his final breath.

conclusion: Antoni Gaudí turned craft into prophecy, reshaping Barcelona with structures that feel grown rather than built. His unfinished Sagrada Família stands as his truest signature—an enduring faith in form, labor, and imagination.

events.date_note: Sources disagree on whether he was born in Reus or Riudoms; he was baptized the next day in Reus
events.title: Birth in Baix Camp
events.description: Antoni Plàcid Guillem Gaudí i Cornet was born in the [[Baix Camp|Baix Camp]] to coppersmith Francesc Gaudí i Serra and Antònia Cornet i Bertran. His birthplace is disputed between the neighboring towns of Reus and Riudoms, a controversy that persists due to missing documentation. He was baptized the following day at the church of Sant Pere in Reus.

Baix Camp.explanation: A comarca (county-level administrative region) in Catalonia that includes towns such as Reus and Riudoms, where Gaudí’s birthplace is traditionally placed.

events.title: Moves to Barcelona to study
events.description:
In 1868, as a teenager, Gaudí moved from the Reus/Riudoms area to Barcelona to continue his education, including a period studying teaching at the Convent del Carme. The change put him inside the city that would become the main stage for his career, where learning happened as much through workshops and draftsmen’s tables as through classrooms.

In these student years he also tested ideas far beyond architecture. Alongside fellow students Eduard Toda i Güell and Josep Ribera i Sans, he became interested in utopian socialism and even sketched an unrealized plan to restore Poblet Monastery as a utopian phalanstère—a youthful experiment in imagining how buildings might reorganize everyday life.

phalanstère.explanation: A planned communal-living complex proposed by the French utopian socialist Charles Fourier—meant to reshape society through shared work and domestic life.

events.title: Completed military service
events.description: Between 1875 and 1878, Gaudí completed his compulsory military service with an infantry regiment in Barcelona, serving as a Military Administrator. Most of this period was spent on sick leave, which allowed him to continue his architectural studies instead of serving on campaign.

events.title: Graduates as an architect
events.description:
In 1878, Gaudí graduated from the Barcelona Higher School of Architecture, supporting himself along the way as a draughtsman for architects and builders. The school’s director, Elies Rogent, later became associated with the famous remark that the degree had been awarded to either a fool or a genius.

That same year, work shown at the 1878 Paris World's Fair helped place him in front of influential future patrons—most notably Eusebi Güell—turning a student’s portfolio into the start of a career-defining patronage network.

Paris World's Fair.explanation: The Exposition Universelle of 1878, a major international exhibition in Paris that showcased industry and the arts and served as a networking venue for artists and designers.

events.title: Won early public commissions
events.description: In his first years as a qualified architect, Gaudí secured visible public work in Barcelona, including decorative lampposts for [[Plaça Reial|Plaça Reial]] and other small projects. These commissions demonstrated his ability to merge utility with striking ornamental design and helped him build credibility in the city’s competitive architectural scene.

images.caption: Plaça Reial lampposts (1879), Gaudí’s first official commission

Plaça Reial.explanation: A central square in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter, redesigned in the 19th century; Gaudí’s first major public commission was the design of its streetlamps (1878–1879).

events.title: Built Casa Vicens
events.description: In Barcelona, Gaudí executed [[Casa Vicens|Casa Vicens]], widely treated as his first major private house commission and a breakthrough in his early career. The project displayed his emerging synthesis of historicist references, local craft traditions, and bold color and surface patterning, and its success helped him attract increasingly ambitious private clients.

images.caption: Casa Vicens, first building projected by Antoni Gaudí

Casa Vicens.explanation: A Gaudí-designed private residence commissioned by stockbroker Manuel Vicens; it is generally regarded as one of his earliest major works in Barcelona.

events.title: Took over Sagrada Família
events.description: In 1883, Gaudí was appointed to take over the still-early [[Basílica i Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família|Sagrada Família]] project in Barcelona after the original architect, [[Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano|Francisco de Paula del Villar]], resigned amid disputes with the promoters. Gaudí abandoned Villar’s initial neo-Gothic plan and reconceived the church on a far more ambitious and personal basis, a commitment that would dominate the rest of his career.
involved_people: Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano

images.caption: Basílica i Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família, Barcelona

Basílica i Temple Expiatori de la Sagrad.explanation: The full official name of the Sagrada Família, a Catholic expiatory basilica in Barcelona financed historically by private donations.

Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano.explanation: The architect originally in charge of the Sagrada Família project who resigned in 1883, leading to Gaudí’s appointment as successor.

events.title: Expanded work with Güell
events.description:
Following his introduction through the 1878 Paris exhibition, Gaudí developed a long collaboration with the industrialist and patron Eusebi Güell. From about 1886 onward, this relationship in [[Modernisme|the modernista style]] Barcelona brought him a stream of commissions—notably Palau Güell (begun 1886) and, later, Parc Güell—where he could push structural and decorative experimentation.

Through Güell’s circle he also found elite clients beyond Barcelona, including Antonio López y López, 1st Marquess of Comillas, for whom he designed El Capricho in Comillas. Güell’s sustained patronage helped consolidate Gaudí’s standing and supported the emergence of his highly personal architectural language.
involved_people: Antonio López y López, 1st Marquess of Comillas

images.caption: Palau Güell (Güell Palace), by Antoni Gaudí, Barcelona

Modernisme.explanation: Catalan Art Nouveau movement (late 19th–early 20th century) closely associated with Barcelona, emphasizing craft, ornament, and new architectural forms.

Park Güell.explanation: A major Gaudí-designed park complex in Barcelona originally conceived as a residential garden city development for Güell; it later became a public park.

events.title: Suffered fasting-related illness
events.description: Gaudí’s Catholic devotion and strict vegetarianism contributed to severe fasting practices. In 1894, a period of intense fasting led to a life-threatening illness, revealing the physical costs of his growing ascetic discipline and foreshadowing the increasingly austere personal life that would accompany his later work.

events.title: Joined Catholic artistic circles
events.description: In 1899, Gaudí joined the Cercle Artístic de Sant Lluc, a Catholic artistic society in Barcelona linked to prominent religious and cultural figures in Catalonia. Through this milieu he connected with influential Catholic thinkers such as Bishop Josep Torras i Bages. The choice fit the direction of his life: a deepening spirituality that increasingly shaped his priorities, his social world, and the symbolism of his work.

images.caption: 1899 Cercle Artístic de Sant Lluc exhibition poster

Cercle Artístic de Sant Lluc.explanation: A Barcelona-based artists' association founded in 1893 with a strong Catholic, moralizing orientation, influential in Catalan cultural life around the turn of the 20th century.

events.title: Won Casa Calvet prize
events.description: In 1900, Gaudí received the [[Barcelona City Council|Barcelona City Council’s]] award for best building of the year for Casa Calvet. The recognition marked a peak of mainstream civic approval at a time when his style was becoming more daring and less conventional, helping consolidate his standing as a leading architect of Barcelona’s modernista era.

Barcelona City Council.explanation: The municipal government of Barcelona (Ajuntament de Barcelona), which awarded annual civic prizes recognizing notable new buildings in the city.

events.title: Developed Park Güell project
events.description: In 1900, Gaudí began designing Park Güell in Barcelona as an intended upscale residential development promoted by Eusebi Güell. Although the urbanization failed commercially, the site evolved into one of his most influential landscape-and-architecture syntheses, integrating structural invention with mosaic and craft work. It showed how he could build an immersive environment—paths, terraces, and ornament working as a single system—rather than a stand-alone monument.

Park Güell.explanation: A public park in Barcelona originally conceived as a private garden-city style housing development (Park Güell estate) commissioned by Eusebi Güell and designed by Antoni Gaudí.

events.date_note: This period groups his two emblematic Barcelona house projects, Casa Batlló (remodeling) and Casa Milà (new construction)
events.title: Created landmark urban houses
events.description:
During these years Gaudí produced two of his most iconic Barcelona works: the transformation of Casa Batlló and the design and construction of Casa Milà. Both projects advanced his shift toward architecture modeled on natural forms, with sculptural façades and bold structural and spatial solutions.

Around this same time he settled in a house within Park Güell, sharing daily life with close family—especially his father, Francesc Gaudí i Serra, and his niece, Rosa Egea Gaudí—and relying on a workshop circle of trusted collaborators as his projects grew more demanding.

images.caption: Casa Batlló, by architect Antoni Gaudí, Barcelona

events.title: Exhibited work in Paris
events.description: In 1910, a major exhibition at the Grand Palais in Paris presented Gaudí’s work through drawings, plans, and plaster models, attracting wider international attention and strong press responses that reinforced his reputation beyond Spain and underscored his move beyond mainstream Modernisme toward a distinct personal idiom.

events.title: Focused entirely on Sagrada Família
events.description:
From 1915, Gaudí devoted his professional life exclusively to the Sagrada Família, directing design decisions through models and on-site problem-solving rather than conventional finished plans. His workshop practice emphasized specialized crafts and a disciplined control of form, structure, and symbolism.

His daily life narrowed as well: in 1925 he moved to live within the Sagrada Família workshop complex, and in this intensely devotional period he even attended a Gregorian chant course taught by the Benedictine monk Gregori M. Sunyol in Barcelona.

images.caption: Urban study of the Sagrada Família by Gaudí (1916)

Sagrada Família.explanation: Large unfinished Roman Catholic basilica in Barcelona (Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família) that became Gaudí’s primary project and where he ran his workshop on site.

events.title: Tram accident and death
events.description: Gaudí was struck by a tram in Barcelona and suffered serious injuries. After several days in hospital, he died on 10 June 1926, shortly before his 74th birthday. His death ended the direct guiding hand behind the Sagrada Família and the mature phase of his architectural experiments.
